The Sharptail mola (Masturus lanceolatus) attains a remarkable ultimate body size, with photographic evidence indicating a total length of 337 cm for a large individual. Applying a standard morphometric conversion to this specimen yields an ultimate standard length of approximately 286.45 cm [Li = approximately 286.45 cm]. This places the species among the largest extant teleosts, rivaling the oceanic sunfish in overall dimensions. The onset of reproductive capability in this species is estimated to occur at a considerably smaller size. Based on comparative life-history data from related tetraodontiform fishes, the standard length at which puberty is reached is thought to be around 100 cm [Lp = around 100 cm]. This marked disparity between size at maturity and maximum size suggests a protracted juvenile growth phase followed by an extended adult period focused on high fecundity. Field observations further indicate that growth trajectories in this species are heavily influenced by oceanographic productivity, with individuals in nutrient-rich waters potentially achieving these dimensions more rapidly than those in oligotrophic environments.

Reproductive output in the Sharptail mola is extraordinary and is closely tied to thermal conditions. Under a stable water temperature regime of 21 °C [T = 21 °C], the maximum daily reproductive rate has been estimated from fecundity data. The species is capable of producing an enormous number of oocytes, with the peak output reaching approximately 684,931 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 684,931 eggs per day]. This value is derived from an annual fecundity estimate that reflects the species' strategy of extreme fecundity, a classic r-selected trait that compensates for high early-life mortality in the pelagic environment. The sheer magnitude of this daily output is unparalleled among bony fishes and underscores the energetic demands placed on a single gravid female. Comparative analyses with other large tetraodontiforms indicate that this reproductive rate is among the highest recorded, consistent with the species' investment in a minimal per-offspring strategy.

Neonatal biology in Masturus lanceolatus begins with a remarkably small propagule. The wet weight at birth, estimated from an egg diameter of 1.3 mm, is just 0.9 milligrams [Wwb = 0.9 milligrams]. This minute mass, less than a thousandth of a gram, is characteristic of species that produce vast numbers of small, pelagic eggs. The tiny yolk-sac larva that emerges following eclosion is entirely reliant on its endogenous reserves before transitioning to first exogenous feeding. The size of the hatchling stands in stark contrast to the adult dimensions, highlighting an extreme disparity in body mass across the life cycle. This life-history strategy prioritizes numerical output over per-offspring investment, a pattern common among large, highly fecund marine teleosts. The high early mortality rate necessitates such a strategy, and the tiny propagule size allows for the production of millions of gametes per breeding season.

Lifespan estimates for the Sharptail mola reveal pronounced sex-specific differences in longevity, which have been modeled under standard thermal conditions. For female individuals, the maximum lifespan is projected at 105 years [am = 105 years] when maintained at a stable temperature of 21 °C [T = 21 °C]. This extraordinary longevity, rivaling that of some marine mammals and deep-sea fishes, suggests a remarkably slow rate of senescence following the attainment of maximum size. Males, by contrast, exhibit a substantially shorter lifespan. The projected maximum longevity for male Sharptail mola is 85 years [am = 85 years] under the same thermal regime at a temperature of 21 °C [T = 21 °C]. This difference of two decades between the sexes may reflect differential energetic investment in reproduction, with females requiring additional energy reserves to support the production of astronomically large numbers of eggs over an extended reproductive lifetime.
